opus-5.5.text:
I think it was a pretty natural transition, and honestly a healthy one. When I started Tianshou, it was very much a personal project. I wanted a reinforcement learning library that was clean, fast, and easy to modify, because a lot of the existing ones at the time felt either too heavy or too hard to hack on for research. So in the early days I wrote most of the code myself, reviewed every PR, and had a very specific picture in my head of what the library should look like.

But at some point you have to be honest with yourself about your bandwidth. After I started working full-time, I just didn't have the same amount of time to respond to issues, review contributions carefully, and keep up with new algorithms. If I had insisted on being the only gatekeeper, the project would have slowed down or quietly died, and that would have been worse for everyone who depends on it.

So handing over maintenance felt less like losing something and more like letting the project grow up. There were people in the community who cared about it a lot, who were already contributing high-quality code and had good taste about the design. Giving them real authority, not just commit access but the ability to make decisions, was the right move. They've pushed it in directions I might not have prioritized myself, like better documentation, more rigorous testing, and broader API support, and that's great.

Of course there's a little bit of an emotional side. It's like something you built yourself, and when other people change things you sometimes think, "Hmm, I would have done that differently." But I think that's exactly the point of open source. A project shouldn't depend on one person's taste or one person's schedule. If it can survive and improve without you, that means it actually became useful to people. For me, that's probably the best outcome I could have hoped for.

r001.rationale: The candidate says community maintainers received authority to make decisions, but does not state that one person having final decision-making authority is sufficient to keep community-led maintenance consistent.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it felt a bit like letting go of something I'd been holding onto too tightly. I started Tianshou when I was an undergrad at Tsinghua, and for a long time it was basically my project. Every issue, every pull request went through me. That works when you have the time and the energy, but at some point I moved on to other things, first at OpenAI and then elsewhere, and I just couldn't give it the attention it deserved. Users were waiting days or weeks for a response, and that's not fair to a community that's actually relying on your code.

So the shift was partly necessity, but I also think it was the right thing philosophically. An open-source project isn't really mine once other people depend on it. If I'm the single point of failure, then the project's health is tied to my calendar, which is a bad design, the same way you'd never want that in software. Giving maintainers real authority, not just commit access but the ability to make decisions about direction, was the only way for it to keep evolving.

What surprised me was how much better some things got without me. The new maintainers refactored parts of the codebase I'd been reluctant to touch because of sunk cost. They brought in ideas from their own research that I wouldn't have prioritized. There were moments of discomfort, seeing a design choice I'd have made differently, but I had to remind myself that a project that only reflects one person's taste is a fragile project.

The lesson I'd pass on is that handing over control is a skill you have to practice deliberately. It means writing down the implicit knowledge in your head, trusting people before you're fully comfortable, and resisting the urge to step back in every time something diverges from your vision. The payoff is that the thing you built actually outlives your personal involvement, and that's really the point of open source.

r001.rationale: The response says maintainers need authority to make decisions about the project’s direction, but it does not state that one person with final decision-making authority is sufficient to keep community-led maintenance consistent.

astra-6.text:
I see it as a natural evolution for an open-source project. When you maintain something yourself, you can move quickly and keep a consistent direction, but you also become a bottleneck. Giving the community maintenance authority means other people can take responsibility and help shape where Tianshou goes.

Of course, that means being willing to let go. People may make different decisions than I would, and I have to be comfortable with that. For me, the important thing is that the project can continue to grow without depending on one person. That’s a healthier future for both the project and its community.

r001.rationale: The response says self-maintenance can keep a consistent direction, but it does not state that one person’s final decision-making authority is sufficient to keep community-led maintenance consistent.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it as a shift from being responsible for everything myself to sharing that responsibility with the community. When you maintain a project on your own, it’s easy for your time and your preferences to become the bottleneck. Giving the community real maintenance authority means accepting that other people may make different decisions—and being comfortable with that.

For me, the important thing is that Tianshou can keep developing without depending on one person. That also changes my role: instead of making every decision, I can help contributors understand the project and feel confident taking ownership. I think that’s a healthy direction for an open-source project.

r001.rationale: The response describes sharing responsibility and allowing contributors to take ownership, but does not say that a person with final decision-making authority is sufficient to keep community-led maintenance consistent.
